content.body:
Phase 2 of [Embedded help](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/project-docs/embedded-help/README.md). The plan is [phase-2-marker-decision.md](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/project-docs/embedded-help/phase-2-marker-decision.md), which has the measurements and the full reasoning. A decision by the maintainer, then one pull request with the decision file; no code.

**What #885's measurements show:** no rule over the prose picks a good summary. Of the docs' 326 entries, the 240 diagnostics' first paragraph is their metadata line (155 have a **When** paragraph; 85 have none); 37 sections open with a paragraph over 300 characters whose first sentence would do; 7 open with a lead-in ending in ":"; 2 have no paragraph first. A summary is something a writer, or an agent, decides.

**Recommended, after discussing it with @KyleBlankRollins:** a section summary, `@summary`, for every section, with `@note`'s two bindings (SPEC §4: "self (with primary), else following block"):

```markdown
## `ascribe versions release`
@id {permalink=true}: cli-versions-release

@summary
Releases a line.

It rewrites each mark's `planned` for its target to the line's version, …
```

```markdown
## ASC149 `page-size`
@id {permalink=true}: ASC149
@summary: A page's Markdown, as a build writes it for agents to read, is as long as the limit or longer.
```

- **`@summary` alone** makes the next block the summary, rendered where it is: a writer picks a sentence the page already shows, so nothing is written twice.
- **`@summary: text`** gives its own text, which the page's body doesn't show, as a page's `description` isn't in its body: for a lead-in or a diagnostic.
- **General, not help's:** any section may have one. Embedded help is its first reader; the JSON output, link hovers, search, and link previews can read it later.
- **Optional, and no guessing:** from phase 3, `help.json`'s `summary` is the section's `@summary` or absent; phase 1's first-paragraph rule goes.
- **Not chosen:** a container (`@summary:` … `@end`), a heading attribute naming a paragraph (`summary=2`), and a `{render=true}` attribute, which would make one attribute change both where the text comes from and whether it shows.

**Also settled, as recommended in the plan:** one summary per section (a second is an error); the line form at the top of its section, the following form before the block it marks; the following form marks a paragraph; the line form's text is inline content; a summary in a fragment is its landing section's; one inside a variant arm is an error until phase 6; the line form writes nothing in the site and plain bodies, the following form's block is written as it is with its own source anchors, and the JSON output carries the summary on the section's heading; the generator writes `@summary:` from each diagnostic's `when`, and the 85 without one get a `when`.

**The one question left for @KyleBlankRollins:** the check for a section with a permalink and no summary. Summaries aren't tied to permalinks; only this check ties them, and only for embedded help. Recommended: **advice by default, configurable in `[checks]`**, so a project that only links to its permalinks isn't asked for summaries, and one that ships embedded help raises it to a warning.

**Done when:** a decision file in `project-docs/decisions/`, numbered by this issue, records the form, each rule, the check's default, and why, and nothing else changes. #880 (phase 3) starts from it.

**Blocked by #878 and #879.** The directive's bindings and rules are whatever #879's decision file settles; don't choose them here.

**What to build:** `@summary`, general to every section, with both bindings (`@summary: text`, its own text not shown in the body; `@summary` alone, the next block, rendered where it is), through syntax, `fmt`, resolve, and the site, plain, and JSON emitters, with its diagnostics. `help.rs` takes the summary from the section's `@summary`, or leaves it absent: decision 10's first-paragraph rule is removed, and `help.json`'s keys don't change. The language server's completion and hover for it. The diagnostics generator writes `@summary: <when>` under each diagnostic's `@id`, and each of the 85 diagnostics without a `when` gets one in `diagnostics.toml`; if those sentences make the pull request too large to read, they go first, in a pull request of their own.

**Done when:**
- After `ascribe build --config docs`, every diagnostic's `help.json` summary is its `when`, and no entry's summary comes from a section without `@summary`.
- Conformance cases for both bindings' parse and canonical form, a summary in a fragment, in a variant arm, two in a section, and each diagnostic; emit tests for each binding, a fragment, and none.
- Site and plain outputs of every project are byte for byte the same where no `@summary` is written; the diagnostics reference's changes are its `@summary` lines and new `when` sentences, named with `--accept`.

- **The editor:** the hover on a section's heading and its `@id` line, and This page's Permalink row tooltip, show the section's summary, from the function `help.rs` uses.

`ascribe rename` refuses a rename that changes only a page's case on a case-insensitive file system, as macOS's APFS and Windows' NTFS are by default.

**Steps:** in a copy of `examples/quill` on macOS, `ascribe rename docs/keys.md docs/Keys.md`.

**What happens:** it refuses, saying "`Keys.md` is there already": the check for an existing destination finds the source itself, since the file system matches names without case.

**Expected:** the page is renamed to `Keys.md`, and the links that name it change, as for any rename. `git mv docs/keys.md docs/Keys.md` does it. The language server's move (`crates/ascribe-lsp/src/rename.rs`, `file_move`) and the CLI's (`crates/ascribe-cli/src/commands/rename.rs`) likely share the check; the editor's Explorer rename should be tried too.

Found by the redirects proposal's spike (`project-docs/proposals/redirects.md`), whose moves table relies on a case-only rename working. **Done when:** a case-only rename of a page and of a fragment works on a case-insensitive file system, with a test that runs where the CI matrix has one (Windows on pull requests that touch paths, macOS after the merge), and a move onto a different file whose name differs only in case is still refused; a changelog entry in `changes/fixes/`.

content.body:
With `[consumer] trailing-slash = "never"`, `@ascribed/astro` gives Astro `trailingSlash: "never"` but leaves `build.format` at Astro's default, `directory`, so each page is written as `x/index.html`. A static host serves that file at `/x/`, not `/x`, so the address Ascribe publishes for every page answers with a 301.

**Steps:** build `examples/astro-site` (`pnpm build`), whose `ascribe.toml` sets `trailing-slash = "never"` and `base-path = "/docs/"`, put `dist/` under `docs/`, and deploy it to Netlify.

**What happens:**

- `dist/guides/my-setup/index.html`'s canonical link and `sitemap.xml` say `https://docs.example.com/docs/guides/my-setup`.
- Netlify answers `/docs/guides/my-setup` with `301 → /docs/guides/my-setup/`, and serves the page only there. A link, the sitemap, and the canonical all point at a redirect, and search engines see the canonical disagree with the served address.
- Netlify's `pretty_urls = false` (`[build.processing.html]` in `netlify.toml`) changes nothing. A page written as `x.html` is served at `/x` with a 200, and `/x/` redirects to `/x`.

**Expected:** a page's published address is served with a 200. For `trailing-slash = "never"`, the integration sets Astro's `build.format` to `"file"`, so pages are written as `x.html`; a site that sets `build.format` itself to something that disagrees fails the build, as `site`, `base`, and `trailingSlash` do. `always` stays `directory`. The integration's `updateConfig` call is in `packages/astro/src/index.ts`; the copied plain output (`x.md` beside `x.html`) and `_ascribe/files/` need checking under the new layout, and the home page under a base path (`/docs` rather than `/docs/`).

Found by the redirects proposal's host test on Netlify (`project-docs/proposals/redirects.md`, "What a real host showed"): a redirect to such a page costs two hops. Ascribe's own docs and site use `always`, so they aren't affected; any project on `never` is, on Netlify and on any host that serves `x/index.html` at `x/`.

content.body:
The daily docs report (#933) said `llms-txt-links-resolve` warned with "49/50 same-origin sampled links resolve (98%); 1 broken; 1 failed to fetch", asked us to report it as a bug in Ascribe, and named no link. Investigating took a fresh run of afdocs: the link was one fetch that failed, and every link resolved the next day. Three changes would have made the report say that itself.

**1. Name the links.** afdocs' JSON gives each check a `details` object; for `llms-txt-links-resolve` it holds `sameOrigin.broken` and `crossOrigin.broken`, each a list of `{ url, status, error }`. `crates/ascribe-check/src/site.rs` deserializes only `id`, `category`, `status`, and `message` (`CheckResult`), so the addresses are lost. ASC171's `{result}` should list each one: the address and its HTTP status for a broken link, or the address and the error for one that failed to fetch. Other checks whose `details` name addresses can follow the same pattern; this one is the case that's bitten.

**2. Don't send a fetch error to the issue tracker.** In afdocs 0.22.2's source, `broken` is every link that didn't come back OK, and `fetchErrors` counts the subset that failed with an error rather than a status. When every failure is a fetch error, nothing Ascribe wrote is wrong yet: ASC171 should say the links couldn't be fetched, name them, and say to run the report again, without "Report it at …". A link with an HTTP status keeps today's message.

**3. Fix "no longer fails" for a check that went from fail to warn.** `crates/ascribe-cli/src/commands/report/text.rs` (around line 713, "{resolved} that failed on {since} no longer {}") counts only `fail` as failing, so a check that moved from `fail` to `warn` is listed as no longer failing while the same report lists it under "To change" with a warning. It should say the check now warns instead of failing.

**Done when:**
- A test with a stand-in checker (`SiteChecker`) whose `llms-txt-links-resolve` result has one broken link and one fetch error shows ASC171 naming both, each with its status or error.
- A result whose only failures are fetch errors gives the message without the issue tracker's address.
- The report's history says a check that went from `fail` to `warn` now warns, in its test (`crates/ascribe-cli/tests/all/report.rs`).
- `tests/conformance/diagnostics.toml`'s ASC171 gains the message variant for fetch errors, with the generated diagnostics page blessed.

content.body:
Two systems keep the same promise, that a published link keeps working:

| | Permalinks | Addresses |
|---|---|---|
| Record | `ascribe.permalinks`, plus `[permalinks.retired]` and `[permalinks.aliases]` in `ascribe.toml` | `ascribe.addresses`: `[moved]`, `[retired]`, `[former]` |
| Retire | `ascribe permalinks retire NAME --reason` (edits `ascribe.toml`) | `ascribe addresses retire OLD --reason` (edits `ascribe.addresses`) |
| Gone without a decision | `permalink-removed` | `address-lost`, `anchor-lost` |

SPEC §7.10 carves permalinks out ("A permalink's name is the permalinks list's to keep"). A retired permalink with a `to` is a move in all but name, and a writer meets two retire commands and two record files: one record is in the hand-written config, the other in a file Ascribe writes.

Decision (Kyle): merge them. The spec stays a draft for now, so this can change SPEC §7.5, §7.6, and §7.10.

## Done looks like

- What happened to a permalink (retired with a reason, retired to a new place, aliased) is recorded in `ascribe.addresses`, for example under keys at the permalinks' path. `[permalinks.retired]` and `[permalinks.aliases]` leave `ascribe.toml`, and `ascribe check --fix` or a one-time command moves an existing project's entries.
- `ascribe.permalinks` stays as the published list that a product's `ascribe permalinks verify` checks against, and is still written from the content plus the addresses file.
- One retire command covers both, or `permalinks retire` writes to `ascribe.addresses`. The diagnostics use one word for "gone" (`*-lost` or `*-removed`, not both).
- SPEC, the content model contract, `publishing/redirects.md`, `permalinks/`, the editor's quick fix on `permalink-removed`, the MCP addresses tools, and the agents skill all describe the one model.
- The docs project (`docs/`) moves its two `[permalinks.retired]` entries over.

From the coherence review: [How Ascribe's features fit together](https://claude.ai/artifact/WdVoVdtBH75vVGPFczwUrC), finding 1.

content.body:
Retiring a release line in a project that keeps `ascribe.addresses` loses the line's addresses. All you get is an advice.

Steps, on a copy of `examples/quill` in a fresh git repository:

```sh
ascribe addresses init && git add -A && git commit -m base
ascribe versions retire "self-managed 3.4" --url https://archive.example/3.4/ --force
git commit -am retire
ascribe check --base HEAD~1
ascribe addresses list
```

```text
ascribe.addresses:1: [ASC258] the base has the build `site@3.4`, and ascribe.toml doesn't now, so its 17 addresses aren't compared
No build writes a redirect or a retired address.
```

`versions retire` already works out where each address should go (it prints `/3.4/configure-legacy/  →  /configure/`, and `--format json` lists them all). But `docs/content/versions/release.md:134` says "a host's redirects file is yours to write", which was written before `ascribe.addresses` could make the build write redirects.

## Done looks like

- When the project has `ascribe.addresses`, `versions retire` records the line's addresses there (a `[former]` entry for the line, `[moved]` entries, or whatever form fits SPEC §7.10). The build then writes the redirects `versions retire` computes, and `ascribe addresses list` shows them.
- `ascribe check --base` treats a line that `[releases]` archived as accounted for, and doesn't report `addresses-build-gone` for it.
- Without `ascribe.addresses`, it keeps listing the addresses as it does now.
- `versions/release.md` and `versions/archive.md` say what's recorded.
- A test covers the steps above.

From the coherence review: [How Ascribe's features fit together](https://claude.ai/artifact/WdVoVdtBH75vVGPFczwUrC), finding 2.

`examples/quill/ascribe.toml` makes a version's build in two ways at once. `[builds.site] versions = "self-managed"` makes `site@3.4`. A hand-written `[builds."self-managed-3.3"]` filters `availability = { filter = "self-managed 3.3" }`, but `[releases.self-managed]` has only `live = ["3.4", "3.5"]`, so 3.3 is neither live nor archived.

- `ascribe check` is clean, and `ascribe versions list` doesn't mention the 3.3 build.
- `ascribe versions retire "self-managed 3.4"` refuses because the change would affect `self-managed-3.3`. With `--force`, that build gains `configure.md`, `upgrade.md`, and `webhooks.md`.

- A build whose `availability` filter names a version of a target that `[releases]` lists as neither live, planned, nor archived gets a diagnostic. It could be advice that suggests `versions =` or adding the line to `[releases]`. It goes in the registry, with an `explain` entry.
- Quill uses one model: either 3.3 is an archived line, or the `self-managed-3.3` build goes, and its comments and the render fixtures that depend on it are updated (`tests/render/corpus/quill/`).
- After that, `versions retire "self-managed 3.4"` on quill runs without `--force`.

content.body:
Several words mean different things in different features:

| Word | Meanings in use |
|---|---|
| example | Tested examples (`example-stale`, `example-unobserved`, `ascribe.examples.toml`); OpenAPI JSON examples checked against a schema (`example-schema-mismatch`, `example-not-json`, `example-body-missing`, `example-schema-unsupported`); the docs' Examples section about code; the repo's `examples/` |
| agents | Agents that write docs (`ascribe agents`, the skill, hooks) and agents that read them (`[consumer] agents`, `ascribe report agents`, which runs afdocs on a site, `[former] agents`) |
| report | `ascribe report`, "the project report"; and `diff --format html`, "the review report" |
| review | Pull request review; the `review` next step in a report; `review-overdue` page review dates |
| source(s) | Page source files ("the source index", **Open Source Changes**, an addresses key "is a source"); `[sources.<name>]` and `ascribe sources`, the code the docs show |
| target | A release target; `agents sync --target`; the TARGET argument of `refs`, `link`, `rename` |
| line | A release line; a snippet's "tested line"; a file's line |

`docs/content/glossary.md` has eight terms. Release line, availability, permalink, address, source, memo, baseline, and acknowledgement aren't in it, so Ascribe's own `@term` checking can't hold the docs to one meaning.

## Done looks like

- The glossary has an `@term` entry for each of the core concepts above, with one meaning each.
- For each row of the table, one meaning keeps the word and the others are renamed in diagnostics, report sections, flags, and docs. Proposed: the OpenAPI slugs become `api-example-*` (or `sample-*`), the report section `agents` becomes `delivery`, the review report gets a name without "report", and page review dates become something other than "review" (e.g. `recheck-overdue`). Renamed diagnostic slugs keep their `ASC` codes, and renamed docs anchors are recorded as retired permalinks or moves.
- `design/words.toml` and the agents skill match.

This can be split into a PR per word if that's easier to review.

From the coherence review: [How Ascribe's features fit together](https://claude.ai/artifact/WdVoVdtBH75vVGPFczwUrC), finding 5.

content.body:
**The problem you're trying to solve:**

SPEC.md says "Version 0.1", and §11 says "Changes to the grammar or the built-in vocabulary are made only in new versions of this specification." Since 0.1, `@snippet`, `@memo`, `@term`, `@summary`, and `@operation` joined the built-ins, and `spec = "0.1"` didn't change (decision 689t: `"0.1"` for now). A page written for the earlier 0.1 with a line starting `@summary:` changed meaning when `@summary` arrived. The spec promises a stability it doesn't give.

**Decision (Kyle, 26 October 2026):** keep the spec a draft until 1.0 rather than cut 0.2.

**Done when:**

- The header and §11 say the specification is a draft: its grammar and built-in vocabulary may grow until 1.0, and `spec = "0.1"` names the draft, not a frozen version. §11 says what 1.0 will promise (changes only in new versions), so the current sentence moves to the future rather than being dropped.
- §3.2's "The keyword set is closed: it grows only by revisions to this specification" reads consistently with the draft status.
- The decision is recorded in `project-docs/decisions/` with the change, since SPEC.md is a contract, and decision 689t's "for now" points to it.
- A changelog entry in `changes/`.

Found while looking for tensions between features and the spec ([write-up](https://claude.ai/artifact/DLzosEjitkNiiboxykapUA)).

The content model reference and its contract are split into `content.md`, `output.md`, `checks.md`, and `validation.md`, and newer sections went wherever there was room:

- `content-model/checks.md` (and `contracts/content-model/checks.md`) holds `[permalinks]`, `[crawlers]`, `[listing]`, and `[apis]`, none of which are checks. `output.md` holds `[sources]`.
- `content-model/index.md`'s description still says "content types, dimensions, availability, phrases, widgets, and builds".
- `contracts/json-reports/sources.md` holds `init`, `sources`, `observe`, and `permalinks`.
- SPEC §7.5 to §7.11 are in arrival order.

content.body:
**The problem you're trying to solve:**

Five passages of SPEC.md describe the toolchain as it was, not as it is. Each is a wording change; no behavior changes.

1. **§9.3's builds example is YAML.** The content model is TOML (§7.1), and every example writes `[builds.<name>]` tables. Rewrite it as TOML, ideally as a `@snippet`-backed example of `examples/quill/ascribe.toml` so it can't drift.
2. **§7.3 says "A processor reads both files and MUST NOT run any command in them."** `ascribe observe` runs the config's commands. `docs/content/contracts/tested-examples.md:15` already scopes the rule to `check`, `build`, `sources`, and the editor. Scope the spec sentence the same way: checking and building never run a command; only a command the person runs to observe examples does.
3. **§9.4 says the site output "depends on no consumer component system."** Heading ids, glossary terms, and links out of a line are `<ascribe-attributes>` markers (site-render contract §2), and a tested block needs the renderer to build its `<figure>` (§5.1). Say that the site output is markdown, custom elements, and attribute markers, and that a consumer applies the markers, with `render_site_html` or the Astro plugin; otherwise someone feeds it to plain remark and loses every explicit heading id.
4. **§10 says "dimension values and lifecycle states have no definition"**, and its first non-normative note says go to definition in `ascribe.toml` "currently recognizes `[phrases]` and `[features.<key>]` table forms only." `crates/ascribe-lsp/src/definition.rs:186–210` goes to features, dimensions, dimension values, note types, widgets, builds, and types. Update the list and drop the stale note (implementation notes belong in the editor docs).
5. **§1.2 principle 7 and §9.1 say the editor reports exactly what a command-line check reports.** `docs/content/editor/problems.md` says otherwise, correctly: the editor shows the editor build only, project-wide checks run on save, and the image checks run only in `ascribe check`. Amend §9.1 and §10 to: the same rules, from the same code; an authoring environment MAY defer project-wide checks and other builds' checks, and SHOULD say when it has (as the status bar's "problems: this build only" does).

**Done when:** each passage says what's true, with a decision file recorded for the change (SPEC.md is a contract) and a changelog entry. `cargo test -p ascribe-conformance` still passes, since the registry test reads SPEC.md.

content.body:
The commands disagree on a few shared flags:

- **Write nothing:** `--check` (`fmt`, `permalinks sync`, `agents sync`, `observe`) and `--dry-run` (`versions release`, `versions retire`). Other commands that write have neither: `rename`, `addresses move` and `retire`, `permalinks retire`, `templates eject`, `check --fix`, `baseline write`.
- **Fail on findings:** `--check`, `--exit-code` (`diff`, `drift`, `templates status`), `--exit-code=<level>` (`report`), `--deny-warnings` (`check`).
- **Safety:** only `versions release` and `retire` refuse, without `--force`, to write files git can't put back.
- **JSON:** `rename`, `sources fetch`, `templates list`, `vale eject`, `agents sync`, and `agents prompt` have no `--format json`.

The project-root files have no naming rule either: `ascribe.nav` is TOML without an extension, `ascribe.examples.toml` has one, `templates.lock` has no `ascribe.` prefix. A name doesn't tell you whether you edit the file or Ascribe writes it.

## Done looks like

- The conventions are written down in CONTRIBUTING.md (or `project-docs/`): every command that writes takes `--dry-run` and the git guard with `--force`; `--check` means a dry run that exits 1 when something would change; `--exit-code[=level]` means "exit 1 on findings", with `--deny-warnings` kept as an alias of `--exit-code=warning` or explained; every command takes `--format json` unless it only prints a file; a file name rule for new project files.
- The commands above follow them. Renamed flags keep their old spelling as a hidden alias for a release.
- A test over the clap definitions holds the conventions, as `names.rs` holds element names.
- Existing files keep their names (renaming them costs every project a migration). The rule applies to new ones.

From the coherence review: [How Ascribe's features fit together](https://claude.ai/artifact/WdVoVdtBH75vVGPFczwUrC), findings 9 and 10.

**The problem you're trying to solve:**

SPEC §3.3 says "Attributes use one grammar everywhere: after a directive name, after an image, and at the end of a table row's first cell." Fence info strings now carry a second attribute language that's in no grammar:

- `phrases=true` (§5.1: the info string "contains the word")
- `title="…"` and `tested="…"`, which `@snippet` writes (§4.8)
- `request="<link>"` and `response="<link> <status> [media type]"` (§7.11)

Each is read by its own code; `request` and `response` are parsed by hand in `crates/ascribe-resolve/src/index/examples.rs:144`. Appendix A has no rule for any of them, so it's unclear whether a quoted value may hold `\"`, whether order matters, what an unknown key means, or whether `phrases = true` with spaces counts.

**What you'd like Ascribe to do:**

Add one section to the spec, say §3.3.1 "Info-string attributes": after the language word, space-separated `key=value` pairs where a value is a token or a double-quoted string (with the escapes §3.3 allows, or none, stated); the keys a processor reads (`phrases`, `title`, `tested`, `request`, `response`); and that other words are left to the consumer. Add its ABNF to Appendix A. If the hand parsers disagree with the rule chosen, bring them in line in the same change, with conformance cases.

**The problem you're trying to solve:**

Parts of `ascribe.toml` and of the diagnostics registry live only in the implementation, while the registry cites spec sections as if the spec defined them:

- `[checks]` and its levels, `[checks.vale]`, `[checks.links]`, `[editor]`, and a content type's `template` and `guide` aren't in SPEC §7.2's table. The content model contract's §26 map, which says "every declaration SPEC §7.2 lists … maps to one section," has no row for `[checks]`.

Add a row to SPEC §7.2 for processor settings: the content model MAY hold settings a processor defines for its own checks and tools, which this specification doesn't, and a processor ignores settings it doesn't know only where it says so. content.body:
**The problem you're trying to solve:**

SPEC §4.9 says only a review check can be acknowledged, and "a problem that makes a document non-conforming never can"; §1.3 and §8.2 say an error makes a document non-conforming and fails a build. `[checks]` lets a project raise a review check to `"error"` (content model contract §19). A project that sets `page-orphan = "error"` now has an error that fails the build and that `@intended` can still acknowledge. "Error" means two things, and the spec mentions neither `[checks]` nor `ascribe.baseline`.

There are four ways to quiet a problem, each with its own rules:

| Mechanism | Scope | Needs a reason | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@intended`, `intended:` frontmatter, `[[intended]]` | One problem, kept for good | Yes | Everything |
| `[checks] <slug> = "off"` | A check, project-wide | No | Everything |
| `[checks] <slug> = "error"` | Raises a review check | No | Everything |
| `ascribe.baseline` | Many advice, for now | No | `check`, editor, hooks, MCP; not `build` or `report` (#976) |

**What you'd like Ascribe to do:**

- In SPEC §8.2 (or §1.3), distinguish the spec's errors, which make a document non-conforming and are never quieted, from a project's levels for review checks, which the project may raise, lower, or turn off, and which can be acknowledged or put in a baseline at whatever level. A raised review check fails a build as an error does, without making the document non-conforming.
- One docs page (or a section of `checks/check.md`) that compares the four mechanisms, from the table above, in place of the partial comparisons in `checks/baseline.md` and `writing/directives.md#intended`.

**Done when:** the spec says it, the docs page exists and the others link to it, with a decision file and a changelog entry.

content.body:
**The problem you're trying to solve:**

The design principles in SPEC §1.2 and the summary of binding in §3.8 were written for the first vocabulary, and newer features strain them:

1. **Principles 2 and 3** ("never what it computes"; "no computed content"). `@operation` writes a method, path, and summary read from an OpenAPI file; marked JSON examples are validated against a schema the spec translates from OpenAPI (§7.11); glossary terms are linked in prose the author never marked (§5.4); `planned` stands for a version from `[releases]`, and `ascribe versions release` rewrites it in source. None adds logic, but a reader of §1.2 would predict none of them. Restate principle 3 as what's held: authors write no logic; anything derived comes from something the content model declares (a registry, a source, an API) and is the same for every reader of a build.
2. **§3.8's "at the top of a section, a directive describes the section; anywhere else, it describes the block it touches."** Following-form `@summary` touches a paragraph anywhere in a section and describes the section (§4.12), and a container that binds (`@memo`) measures touching from its `@end`. Both are paragraphs after the binding table, not rows in it. Add both to the binding table and to §4's table, and say the summary sentence has these exceptions.
3. **"Advice" isn't in §1.3.** Conformance defines errors and warnings; the third severity, used by 61 of 274 diagnostics, first appears in §8.2's introduction. Define it in §1.3.
4. **§1.4 says the spec doesn't depend on table extensions,** but row availability (§4.4) and the plain output's column alignment (§9.4) exist only with GFM tables. Say once in §1.4 that those rules apply where tables are supported.
5. **§4.10 "Nothing reads a memo"** already has two exceptions (`Generated from` memos, and memo files' `quote`, §7.7). Reword to "no processor resolves or publishes a memo," and say when to use `@memo` (a line or two in place) and when a memo file (anything longer).

**Done when:** the five passages are rewritten, with a decision file (SPEC.md is a contract) and a changelog entry. No behavior changes.

Found while looking for tensions between features and the spec ([write-up](https://claude.ai/artifact/DLzosEjitkNiiboxykapUA)).

There's no path for a team that already has Markdown docs. The guides have no page on bringing a folder over, and `ascribe init` makes the first check worse than the language requires:

- The spec gives a project that declares no types an implicit `page` type, whose pages need no `type:`.
- `init` writes `[types.page.frontmatter]`, so the project declares a type, and every existing page fails:

```text
[ASC196] Error: this page doesn't say what type it is; give it `type:` in its frontmatter, with one of: page
```

A folder of 300 pages starts with at least 300 errors, plus a `title` error on each page without frontmatter.

## Done looks like

- `ascribe init` in a folder that already holds Markdown (or with `--content-root` pointing at one) says how many pages it found, and writes an `ascribe.toml` that leaves out `[types]`, so the implicit type applies and no page needs `type:`.
- Where pages have no `title` in frontmatter, init says how many and how to fix them all at once (a fix `ascribe check --fix` can apply from the first heading, or a documented reason why not).
- init ends by running the check and printing a short summary: errors by code, most common first, with the next command to run. Existing advice can go into `ascribe.baseline` with one command it names.
- A how-to, "Bring existing docs to Ascribe", walks a folder of plain CommonMark from `init` to a green `ascribe check`, and says what changes for links, frontmatter, and admonitions written in another tool's syntax. Whether it names those tools is Kyle's call (story decision 4 keeps other tools off the site).
- A test runs `init` on a fixture folder of plain Markdown and holds its output.

`ascribe search` matches a block only when it has every word of the query, each as a substring, with no word forms (`crates/ascribe-query/src/search.rs`). The rules and the skill tell an agent to run it before writing a page about a subject, and an agent asks in natural words. In the Quill example:

```
$ ascribe search "webhook signature"
No place matches.
The words aren't in any page.
$ ascribe search "webhooks signing"
No place matches.
```

`docs/keys.md` has a section called "Sign webhook events" ("A key also signs the events the agent sends to your webhooks"). `signature` and `signing` aren't substrings of `sign`/`signs`, so the agent is told the subject is new and writes a duplicate page. Searching for one word, `sign` or `webhook`, finds it. The answer gives no next step. The MCP tool `ascribe_search` gives the same answer.

## Done looks like

- When no block has every word, the answer lists the blocks that have the most of them, ranked, under a line that says they're partial matches and which words each lacks (for example "No block has both words. These have 1 of 2: …"). Text and JSON both carry it. In JSON it's a new field, so `places` keeps its meaning, and the schema and `docs/content/contracts/` change with a recorded decision.
- Optionally, words match their common forms (`sign`, `signs`, `signing`, `signature`), or the PR says why not.
- `exit 1` stays for "no full match", so scripts don't change.
- A test holds `"webhook signature"` against Quill finding `keys.md#sign-webhooks` as a partial match.
- `docs/content/command/questions.md#cli-search` and the skill's search line say what a partial match is.

content.body:
A writer bringing pages over from a GitHub README or wiki writes GitHub's alert syntax:

```markdown
> [!NOTE]
> Widgetly is in beta.
```

Ascribe says nothing. The site shows a plain block quote that starts with the text "[!NOTE]", and the plain Markdown output escapes it to `> \[!NOTE\]`, so it doesn't render as an alert on GitHub either. `ascribe check` already says "did you mean `@note {type=tip}:`?" for `@tip`; an alert deserves the same.

GitHub's five kinds map onto `@note`'s types one to one: `NOTE`, `TIP`, `IMPORTANT`, `WARNING`, `CAUTION`.

Reproduced on 0.4.4 and on main (887c0a2). (The wider migration path for existing Markdown is the product designer review's to file; this issue is the alert syntax alone.)

## Done looks like

- A block quote whose first line is `[!NOTE]`, `[!TIP]`, `[!IMPORTANT]`, `[!WARNING]`, or `[!CAUTION]` (any case, as GitHub accepts) gets a warning with a code of its own, configurable in `[checks]`.
- Its fix rewrites the quote as `@note {type=<kind>}:` for one paragraph, or the `@note {type=<kind>}:` … `@end` container for several blocks, keeping the content. It's marked safe, so `ascribe check --fix` and the editor's quick fix apply it.
- A block quote that only mentions `[!NOTE]` later in its text isn't reported.
- Conformance cases for each kind, the one-paragraph and container forms, and the non-match; the diagnostics reference, the surface map, and a `changes/` entry.

content.body:
From the architecture review (finding A1). Large; it likely wants a decision in `project-docs/decisions/` before it's split into pull requests.

## What's wrong

A loaded project is three types and three long-lived caches:

- `ascribe_check::Project` holds the model, the source texts, and the side files. `ascribe_resolve::Project` is the index. `IncrementalProject`, wrapped by the language server's `Core`, is a third, live form.
- `Project::index` (`crates/ascribe-check/src/project.rs:666`) builds the index from the file system rather than the texts already held, so `build`, `diff`, `drift`, `sources`, `outline`, `link`, `refs`, `resolve`, and `search` read and index every source twice. The page checks build another through `held_index` (`crates/ascribe-check/src/page/bridge.rs`) unless given one. A file changed between the two reads gives the checks and the build different text.
- Three processes keep a project warm, each its own way: the language server (incremental), the MCP server's cache (`crates/ascribe-cli/src/mcp/cache.rs`, which reloads everything when a listing of files differs), and the hook's check server (`crates/ascribe-cli/src/agents/checker.rs`, which wraps both).

## What to do

One `Workspace` type, beneath the surfaces, that owns the content model, the side files, and an `IncrementalProject`. A command loads one per run and hands it to every library call; the MCP server and the hook server keep one alive and apply changes to it; the language server wraps it with its open buffers. `ascribe_check::Project` becomes a view over it, or goes.

## Done when

- Each command reads each source file once per run, and indexes once: a test counts the reads through a counting `FileSystem`.
- The MCP cache and the hook server keep the project the same way, through the same type, and update it incrementally instead of reloading on a changed listing.
- ARCHITECTURE.md's "Loading a project, and reading files" describes one path, and no longer says the commands index twice.
- No output changes (`node scripts/compare/outputs.ts --base main`), and the corpora benchmarks are no slower.

Related: the split of `ascribe-check` filed alongside this moves project loading out of that crate, and the two are easiest together.

AGENTS.md and the skill tell an agent "Write the phrase (`{product}`), not the text it stands for", but no check holds it. In a review I wrote "Quill" three times and "Quill Cloud" once on a Quill page, and "Ascribe 0.4.4" on a page in `docs/`, where `{version}` is `0.4.4`. `ascribe check` reported nothing. ## Done looks like

- A new diagnostic (for example `phrase-text-written`, advice by default, configurable in `[checks]`) reports prose text that equals a declared phrase's value, outside code and outside a heading the page marks. It's added to `tests/conformance/diagnostics.toml` and `diagnostics.rs` in order, with a conformance case.
- Its fix replaces the text with `{key}`. The fix is `safe` for values that can't be ordinary words (a version, a URL, a value of two or more words), and `unsafe` otherwise. A one-word value matches only whole words, case as written.
- When one value is inside another (`Quill` inside `Quill Cloud`), only the longer one is reported.
- The edit hook reports it with its fix when the fix is safe, as it does other safe advice.

content.body:
Leaving out the braces is the most natural mistake in the language:

```markdown
@note type=warning: You need Node 20.

## Install
```

gives two errors:

```text
[ASC015] Error: `@note` applies to the next block, and the next block here is a heading; a directive can't be bound to a heading
   Help: Move the directive below the heading, directly above the block it describes.
[ASC120] Error: `type=warning: You need Node 20.` isn't part of `@note` …
   Help: Remove `type=warning: You need Node 20.`
```

ASC015 follows from ASC120 and sends the writer the wrong way. ASC120's fix, which `--format json` carries as a code action (`applicability: "unsafe"`) and the editor offers, removes the note's text along with the bad attribute.

Reproduced on 0.4.4 and on main (887c0a2).

## Done looks like

- When a directive line's extra text starts with `key=value` pairs whose keys are attributes of that directive, ASC120's message says the attributes need braces, and its fix rewrites the line as `@note {type=warning}: You need Node 20.`. That fix is safe when everything after the pairs is a `:` and a primary.
- A line ASC120 reports isn't also reported by a binding check (ASC015 and its kin) for the same line.
- Extra text that isn't attributes keeps today's message, and its "Remove" fix stays unsafe.
- Conformance cases: one attribute, two, a key the directive doesn't take, and the container form (`@note type=warning:` with content up to `@end`). The diagnostics reference and a `changes/` entry.

**Problem.** A page's output depends on the spec declared in `[apis]`: `@operation` writes the operation's method, path, summary, and "(deprecated)", and a link to an operation writes its address. `ascribe diff` doesn't treat the spec as something a page depends on, so a spec change that changes a published page goes unreported.

To reproduce (0.4.4 and main at 887c0a2): a page with `@operation: ../../api/openapi.yaml#createWidget`, commit, then change `createWidget`'s `summary` in the spec. `ascribe resolve` shows the new line, `POST /widgets: Make a widget`, but `ascribe diff --base HEAD` lists no change for that page, and `ascribe diff --base HEAD guides/api.md` says "no changes". A reviewer reading the diff never sees that a spec edit changed the guides. Snippets are already tracked this way ("1 changed (through code:src/client.ts#get-widget)").

**Done looks like**

- `ascribe diff` compares each page's output with the base's spec and the working tree's, and lists a page whose output changed through the spec, naming it: "1 changed (through api/openapi.yaml#createWidget)". The same holds for `--format json`, `--format prompt`, and the review preview.
- A spec change that changes no page's output (a schema, a description) lists nothing.
- A test covers a summary change, a `deprecated` change, and an `operationId` rename, each through `@operation` and a plain link.

content.body:
From the architecture review (finding A3).

## What's wrong

`ascribe-check` holds four jobs:

1. The checks, file-level and page-level.
2. Loading a project from disk (`ascribe_check::Project`, `locate`, `load_model`), which is why `ascribe-templates` and `ascribe-query` depend on the checker.
3. Running other programs and remembering their answers: Vale (`prose/`), lychee (`links.rs`), afdocs (`site.rs`), `tool.rs`, `links/cache.rs`, `links/history.rs`, `report_history.rs`, `identity.rs`. Eight of its files write to disk.
4. Composing prompts for agents (`prompt/`).

`ascribe-query`'s report reaches into it for `links`, `site`, `report_history`, and `identity`. The checker also depends on `ascribe-emit` only so the page-size check (`page/size.rs`) can render a page as plain Markdown and measure it.

## What to do

- Project loading moves down, to where the workspace type in #994 lives.
- The tool runners, their caches and histories, and a finding's identity move to an `ascribe-report` crate that `ascribe-query` uses.
- The page-size check takes the measuring function as input, so `ascribe-check` no longer depends on `ascribe-emit`.

## Done when

- `ascribe-check` writes no files: no `fs::write` or `File::create` in `crates/ascribe-check/src`.
- `ascribe-templates` and `ascribe-query` don't depend on `ascribe-check` to load a project, and `ascribe-check`'s `Cargo.toml` doesn't list `ascribe-emit`.
- ARCHITECTURE.md's crate table and dependency list match.
- No output changes (`node scripts/compare/outputs.ts --base main`).

**Problem.** Ascribe reads `ascribe.examples.toml` and `examples.observations/` only at the root of a source's `path`. One put in a subfolder, beside the tests it runs, is ignored without a word: `ascribe observe` runs there and writes its observation, but no page gets a "Tested with" line, and `ascribe check` says nothing.

To reproduce (0.4.4): `[sources.code] path = "."` with `include = ["src/**", "examples/**"]`, and `examples/ascribe.examples.toml`. Run `ascribe observe --yes` in `examples/` (it passes and writes `examples/examples.observations/default.toml`), then `ascribe build`: the snippets of `code:examples/…` have no tested line. It works only after declaring `examples/` as a second source, `[sources.ex] path = "examples"`, which overlaps the first, also without comment.

**Done looks like**

- `ascribe check` reports an `ascribe.examples.toml` inside a source's folder (below its root) that no source's root holds, at the file, with a fix: declare a source whose `path` is that folder, or move the file to the source's root. The editor shows the same.
- `ascribe observe` prints the same warning when run in a folder that is no source's root, after writing the observation, so the person running it learns why no page will show it.
- The [tested examples page](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/docs/content/examples/tested.md) says, in step 1, that the file goes at the source's root and what to do when the tests live in a subfolder.

From the architecture review (finding A6).

## What's wrong

A project has about ten files beside its sources: `ascribe.toml`, `ascribe.lock`, `ascribe.permalinks`, `ascribe.nav`, `ascribe.addresses`, `ascribe.baseline`, `ascribe.examples.toml` and its observations, `templates.lock`, and `memos/`. Each one is added by hand in several places: a text field and a parsed field on `ascribe_check::Project` (`crates/ascribe-check/src/project.rs:234`), a case in the language server's watcher (`crates/ascribe-lsp/src/core.rs`, for example `is_addresses`), a change kind or rule in `crates/ascribe-resolve/src/incremental/mod.rs`, and its checks. Counting files that mention each feature: addresses 64 across 9 crates, permalinks 75 across 9, memos 66 across 11.

## What to do

A `SideFile` trait (its path, how it parses, the issues it raises, and what a change to it invalidates) and a registry of them that the project loader, the language server's watcher, and the incremental layer each go through once. Fewer side files helps as well; #944 folds `ascribe.permalinks` into `ascribe.addresses`.

## Done when

- `ascribe.nav`, `ascribe.addresses`, `ascribe.baseline`, `ascribe.lock`, and `ascribe.permalinks` (or its successor from #944) load, report, and invalidate through the trait.
- Adding a side file touches the registry and the new file's own module, plus its checks; a short section in ARCHITECTURE.md says so.
- No output changes (`node scripts/compare/outputs.ts --base main`).

content.body:
From the architecture review (finding A7).

## What's wrong

Reads go through `ascribe_resolve::FileSystem`, and `crates/ascribe-resolve/tests/all/file_reads.rs` holds that, but there are 81 `Outside FileSystem:` exceptions, and ARCHITECTURE.md lists them in one bullet several hundred words long. Writes have no such door: `fs::write` appears in 8 crates, including the checker's link cache and histories. Edits already follow a better pattern: the library returns each file's text, and the CLI writes it.

## What to do

- Caches and histories (`links/cache.rs`, `links/history.rs`, `report_history.rs`, the MCP and hook servers' cache folders) take a small writer from their caller instead of writing themselves, so a test can hold them in memory.
- A test like `file_reads.rs` for writes: a library write outside the allowed places fails it, with an `Outside FileSystem:`-style comment for each that stays.

content.body:
Every docs URL the CLI hands an agent is a permalink: `ascribe --help`'s "Documentation:", `ascribe explain`'s `docs`, and the diagnostics' links (`https://ascribed-dev.com/go/ASC036/`). `packages/astro/src/Permalink.astro` serves each one as an HTML page with `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` and a script. Most agent fetchers, such as curl and WebFetch-style tools, don't follow a meta refresh. An HTTP fetch also never sends the `#ASC036` fragment. So the agent spends a second fetch and lands on the whole 49 KB `checks/diagnostics/pages/` page, not the section.

Content negotiation doesn't help. With `Accept: text/markdown`, `site/netlify/edge-functions/markdown.ts` looks for `/go/ASC036.md`, which isn't written, and answers with the redirect's HTML.

The parts already exist:

- With `[consumer] host = "netlify"`, the build writes `_ascribe/host/_redirects` (`crates/ascribe-emit/src/site/redirects.rs`). It holds a permalink only under a *former* permalinks path, never today's, and for the docs it's empty.
- `/go/<name>.json` holds the section's text as `help.json` gives it, but nothing points to it.

## Done looks like

- With a host that takes redirects (`host = "netlify"` today), each permalink with a `to` is a `301` line in the `_redirects` the build writes, to its page's address (the fragment can stay in the target, as Netlify keeps it). A retired permalink keeps its page, served with a `410` or `404`. The HTML forwarding page stays for hosts without redirects and for `?platform=` choices. Any rule that needs the page instead (the query parameters) is said in the PR.
- An agent can get the section, not the page, in one fetch: `/go/<name>.md` is published, the section as the plain output writes it, as `help.json`'s `text` is. The forwarding page and the `.json` say so with `<link rel="alternate">`, `type="text/markdown"` and `type="application/json"`. Then the edge function's `.md` lookup finds it with no change.
- The output-layout contract and `publishing/redirects.md` / `permalinks/` say what's written, and `site/test/negotiation.test.ts` covers `/go/ASC036/` asked for as Markdown.
- `curl -sI https://ascribed-dev.com/go/ASC036/` answers `301` after deploy.

Overlaps #944, which moves permalinks' records into `ascribe.addresses`. Whichever lands second writes the redirects from where the records are then.

From the agent-reader review, [Ascribe's docs, read by an agent](https://claude.ai/artifact/CTJjJSgG38ChxgJhSCUvbo), finding F1.

content.body:
[How review works](https://ascribed-dev.com/go/review-guide/) says a changed block has "the words added highlighted and the words removed struck through". In a paragraph it does. Two cases where it doesn't, both in `ascribe diff --format html`:

1. **Inside `@note`.** Changing `@note {type=warning}: You need Node 20.` to `… Node 22 or later.` gives the note the "Changed" label and nothing else, so the reviewer can't see what changed. The report's data has the words (`"words": {"now": [[14,25]], "was": [[14,16]]}`); they aren't drawn inside `<ascribe-note>`. Notes are where versions and warnings live, which is what a reviewer most needs to see. The other elements that wrap text (tabs, steps, details) are worth checking for the same thing.
2. **A short sentence that grew.** "Run `widgetly uninstall`." to "Run `widgetly uninstall` to remove it." is shown as one block removed and another added, rather than as a change with "to remove it" marked. For a short block, the threshold for calling it a new block seems too eager.

Screenshots are in the review linked below.

## Done looks like

- In the HTML report, the page preview, and the site preview, a changed block inside `@note`, a tab, a step, or `@details` has its added and removed words marked as a paragraph's are. A report fixture covers each.
- A block whose old text is kept whole, with words added (or removed) at one end, is a change with the words marked, whatever its length. Replacing most of a short sentence still counts as removed and added. Tests in `ascribe-diff` cover both.
- A `changes/` entry.

From the technical writer review: [Ascribe, through a technical writer's eyes](https://claude.ai/artifact/UkjiUaoWuGoxZPjjyRRhfr), finding 5.

**Problem.** In CI, `ascribe check`'s problems are only in the job log. The text format draws source snippets and repeats each help, which is long in a log, and `concise` and `json` aren't something GitHub reads. An engineer expects a failing docs check to show on the pull request's lines, as linters and compilers do.

**Done looks like**

The message stays one line, with the help left out.

- `ascribe fmt --check` takes the same format, one annotation per file it would change.

SARIF (for code scanning) can follow later; the workflow commands need no permissions and no upload step.

content.body:
With `[consumer] agents` on, each page's Markdown version is published at its address with `.md`, and `llms.txt` links to those. But every link from one page to another inside the `.md` points at the HTML address. In the docs' build that's all 2,259 links between pages, for example `[Agents in the editor](https://ascribed-dev.com/docs/editor/agents/#agents-in-vs-code)` in `agents/mcp.md`. So an agent that follows a link leaves Markdown on its first hop. Content negotiation brings it back only if its fetcher sends `Accept: text/markdown`, and most don't.

## Done looks like

- In the Markdown a build publishes for agents (the `.md` files beside the site), a link to a page the build publishes points at that page's `.md`, with its fragment (`…/editor/agents.md#agents-in-vs-code`). Glossary links follow the same rule.
- The plain output for other uses (`ascribe build --emit plain` with agents off, and `ascribe resolve`) is unchanged, or the PR says why it changes too.
- An id's fragment means the same thing in the `.md` as on the page, so the fragment lands on the matching heading of the Markdown. A test holds this.
- The output-layout contract and `astro/agents.md` say what the links point to, and the change is recorded as a decision, since it changes an output.

If the decision is to keep HTML links, for example because the canonical address is the HTML, the alternative is one sentence in the pointer each `.md` starts with: "Any page here is also Markdown at its address with `.md`." Either way, the PR settles it.

content.body:
For a link to a heading id that doesn't exist (`link-id-missing`, ASC037), the fixes are candidates ranked by `crates/ascribe-resolve/src/closest.rs`. The ranking puts a worse match first when the right id is longer. In `docs/`, a link to `loop.md#ask-instead` gets these fixes:

1. `loop.md#run-the-loop`
2. `loop.md#ask-instead-of-guessing`
3. `loop.md#fix-it-or-say-its-intended`

An agent that takes `fixes[0]` links to the wrong section. Ids shorten in this way all the time, because agents guess an id from the heading's first words. Also, the concise output, the edit hook, and the MCP `ascribe_check` (concise by default) only say "`agents/loop.md` has no heading with the id `ask-instead`". They don't name any candidate, so the agent needs a second round trip through JSON or `ascribe outline`.

## Done looks like

- An id that the wrong id is a prefix of, or that shares its words in order, ranks above one that's merely close in edit distance. A test holds `ask-instead` → `ask-instead-of-guessing` first, and the Quill cases (`sign-webhook-events` → `sign-webhooks`, `rotate` → `rotate-keys`) still come first.
- When one candidate clearly wins, the message ends with "did you mean `loop.md#ask-instead-of-guessing`?", so the concise form and the hook carry it. The same goes for `link-target-missing` when it has one clear candidate.
- The diagnostics' `.snap` and conformance outputs are re-blessed and reviewed.

**What the page is for.** The HTML shows the page's `description` under its title, and `llms.txt` lists it. content.body:
Getting started installs Ascribe as a dev dependency (`npm install --save-dev @ascribed/cli`), so the command is `npx ascribe` or `pnpm exec ascribe`. The AGENTS.md that `ascribe agents sync` writes tells the agent to run `ascribe check <file> --format concise`, `ascribe search`, `ascribe outline`, and so on, which fail with "command not found" in that project unless the agent guesses. The skill in `.agents/skills/ascribe/` has the same commands.

## Done looks like

- `agents sync` works out how the project runs Ascribe: a `package.json` with `@ascribed/cli` or `@ascribed/astro` in its dependencies gives `npx ascribe`, `pnpm exec ascribe`, or `yarn ascribe` by the lockfile beside it; otherwise `ascribe`. A `--command` option overrides it.
- Every command in AGENTS.md, the skill, and the hook's messages uses it. `ascribe agents sync --check` reports a file written with a different one.
- Tests for npm, pnpm, yarn, and no `package.json`; the agents docs say how the command is chosen; a `changes/` entry.

From the technical writer review: [Ascribe, through a technical writer's eyes](https://claude.ai/artifact/UkjiUaoWuGoxZPjjyRRhfr), finding 8.

content.body:
**Problem.** SPEC §4.8's comment table picks the comment syntax by extension, so files engineers quote often can only be shown whole:

- `Dockerfile`, `Makefile`, `Justfile`, `Containerfile`, `.env`, `.gitignore`: no extension, or a dotfile. `@snippet: code:src/Dockerfile#run` gives "can't have regions, because Ascribe doesn't know the comment syntax of its extension".
- `css`, `scss`, `less`: only block comments (`/* :snippet-start: x */`).
- `graphql`, `gql`, `properties`, `mk`, `dockerfile`: `#`, not in the table.

**Done looks like**

- §4.8 matches a file by its whole name before its extension, with a table of names: `Dockerfile`, `Containerfile`, `Makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `Justfile`, `.env` (and `.env.*`), `.gitignore`, all `#`; and adds `graphql`, `gql`, `properties`, `mk`, `dockerfile` to `#`.
- §4.8 allows a tag in a one-line block comment, `/* :snippet-start: x */`, for `css`, `scss`, and `less` (and `//` too for `scss` and `less`).
- A named file's default `lang` comes from the same table (`dockerfile`, `makefile`), since it has no extension to take one from.
- Conformance cases for each new row, a changelog entry, and the spec's revision note.

Found in the software engineer review: [Ascribe for Engineers](https://claude.ai/artifact/MvULrC1CwyAPwXSP2Arae5).

content.body:
Measured from the built Markdown of the 117 docs pages (code blocks, tables, and lists left out): the median sentence is 22 words, 32 paragraphs run over 150 words, and 6 run over 250. Those are walls of text on the page, and the hardest part of the docs for anyone who isn't an implementer. The six:

| Words | Page | Starts |
|---|---|---|
| 411 | `content-model/content.md` | "A mark does nothing only where no output shows it…" |
| 281 | `checks/report-command.md` | "**`links`** lists every `http` and `https` link…" |
| 230 | `content-model.md` | "**Editing.** A taken key is changed in the file that writes it…" |
| 228 | `editor/preview.md` | "**Ascribe: Open Site Preview** opens the active page…" |
| 226 | `contracts/content-model.md` | "**Rules** (SPEC §7.9)…" |
| 215 | `contracts/content-model/content.md` | "**Rules.** `<target>` MUST be…" |

(Three paragraphs in `editor/sidebar.md` and `review/diff.md` measured 260–318 words because of their images' alt text. #972 covers that page's order, and the alt text is listed in the small-fixes issue.)

## Done when

- No paragraph in a guide or reference page (outside `contracts/`) runs over 150 words. Each long one becomes a lead sentence and a list, a table, or a subsection, with no facts lost.
- The 411-word paragraph in `content-model/content.md` is split by case (when a mark does nothing, what each check reports, when the fix removes the mark), possibly as a table.
- Optional, if it's cheap: the docs' Vale configuration (or a test over `docs/content/`) flags a paragraph over 150 words, so it doesn't come back.
- The site and plain outputs change only in layout, with the same links and ids, and `ascribe check` on the docs is clean.

Related: #956 (content model by job), which may move some of these paragraphs. Do whichever lands second on top of the other.

content.body:
`ascribe mcp`'s `tools/list` is 124,345 bytes for its 12 tools, measured on `main` at `887c0a2`. Of that, `outputSchema` is 74,521 bytes, input schemas 8,461, and descriptions 5,406. `ascribe_check` alone is 13.7 KB and `ascribe_model` 18.3 KB. `crates/ascribe-cli/src/mcp/tools.rs` sets `output_schema` on every tool from the command's full JSON Schema, `$defs` included.

A host that gives the model output schemas spends about 30k tokens on Ascribe before the agent's first call, in every session. Hosts that don't still send and parse them. `resources/list` adds 12.8 KB. At this repository's root it names 26 projects, most of them test fixtures, but a user's repository won't have those.

## Done looks like

- `tools/list` is at most 25 KB for the current tools, and a test holds it to a budget that names the number, so a new tool or field can't silently grow it.
- How that's met is the PR's call, with the reason recorded. Some options:
  - Leave out `outputSchema` and say in each description where the schema is (the JSON report contract's page).
  - Keep only the top-level properties, with `$defs` left out.
  - Keep full schemas only for the tools whose `structuredContent` an agent reads field by field (`ascribe_explain`, `ascribe_outline`, `ascribe_link`).
- Every tool still returns the same `structuredContent`, and the JSON report contract still documents its schema.
- `agents/mcp.md` and `agents/commands.md` say which tools carry an output schema, and the plugin in `plugins/ascribe/` is regenerated if it embeds the list.

Related: #962 renames the tools and adds `ascribe_rename`, which this budget will have to include.

From the agent-reader review, [Ascribe's docs, read by an agent](https://claude.ai/artifact/CTJjJSgG38ChxgJhSCUvbo), finding F5.

content.body:
Small things from one afternoon of writing with Ascribe 0.4.4 (each also on main):

1. `ascribe diff main` says "main isn't a file of the project, now or at the base". It's the git habit; the positional argument is a page.
2. `ascribe fmt --check` says a file "would reformat", but not where or how, so a writer can't fix it by hand or judge whether to run `fmt`.
3. `@Note: …` with a capital is plain text with no warning, while `@notes:` gets "did you mean `@note`".
4. `page-orphan`'s help prints a docs-relative Markdown link into the terminal: ``[`[checks]`](content-model/checks.md#19-checks)``.
5. With `--format concise`, a diagnostic loses its suggested fix, such as "Link to `setup.md#…`", which is the most useful part of the full output for a person and an agent alike.
6. Tabs and the plain output show a dimension's raw values ("mac", "Operating system: mac"). `labels` fixes it, but Getting started's example never shows it, so a first site has lowercase tabs.

## Done looks like

- `ascribe diff <arg>`, when `<arg>` isn't a page but is a revision git knows, says "to compare with `main`, use `--base main`".
- `ascribe fmt --check` lists each change as `file:line` with the line before and after (or a unified diff with `--diff`).
- A line starting with `@` and a known directive's name in another case gets `directive-unknown` with "did you mean `@note`".
- Help text printed in the terminal has no Markdown links: the address of the page, or the plain name of the section.
- `--format concise` keeps a diagnostic's first fix on the line, as `→ Link to setup.md#connect-a-data-source`.
- Getting started's `[dimensions.pm]` example has `labels`, with a sentence on what they label.
- Tests for each, and `changes/` entries.

From the technical writer review: [Ascribe, through a technical writer's eyes](https://claude.ai/artifact/UkjiUaoWuGoxZPjjyRRhfr), finding 10.

content.body:
Small problems a reader of ascribed-dev.com notices, each a few lines:

1. **A wide table that can't be scrolled by keyboard.** `/docs/contracts/assets/` has a table (the 43rd child of the content) that scrolls sideways but can't take focus. axe reports `scrollable-region-focusable`, and it's one of only two axe problems on the site. The fix probably belongs wherever tables get their scroll wrapper, so every wide table is covered.
2. **Leads aren't formatted like the body.** Link to your API reference's description reads "Declare your OpenAPI spec in ascribe.toml, link a guide to an operation by its operationId … the operation's address", with plain names and a straight apostrophe. The body uses code and curly quotes. Check the other pages' `description`s for the same thing.
3. **A title repeated as the first H2.** Publish a site for each version (`versions/release.md`) has the H1 "Publish a site for each version" and then the same words as its first H2, from the how-to template's steps section. Rename the H2 (for example "Steps") or drop it.
4. **A sentence split by a code block.** In Getting started's "Format it", the paragraph after `npx ascribe fmt` starts in lowercase ("rewrites directives and attribute blocks…"). Make it a whole sentence.
5. **Alt text of 130–160 words.** The editor screenshots in `editor/sidebar.md` and `review/diff.md` describe every control in the alt. Give each image a short alt, a sentence or two, and keep the detail in the text or a caption, where a screen reader user can skip it.

## Done when

- axe (WCAG 2.1 AA and best practice) reports nothing on `/docs/contracts/assets/`, and a wide table anywhere on the site can be scrolled with the keyboard.
- Items 2 to 5 are fixed as described, and `ascribe check` on the docs is clean.

content.body:
Small things the agent-writer persona review tripped on. Each one is a wording or output fix, with no new feature.

1. **`check`'s summary line.** "checked 9 files for every build, reported on 9: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 3 advice" came from a run where every problem was in one file. "Reported on" counts the files in scope (`files_reported`), but it reads as files with problems.
2. **The rules' generic examples.** In `docs/`, the `@available` line's example is `cloud, self-managed preview 3.4`, but that project has neither target. The rules list a dimension's name ("Here: dimensions `pm`, `release`") but not its values, so the agent has to call `ascribe model` just to write a `@variant`. The check line starts "Programmatic check:", an odd label.
3. **The `new-page` prompt.** For a type with no template, it says "fill in each empty field" when the frontmatter it shows has no empty field. The MCP prompt's `path` argument says the default is "the type's first folder in the project", but `docs/content/agents/commands.md` says the content root. One of them is wrong.
4. **Help text in JSON.** A diagnostic's `help` has relative Markdown links, such as `[[checks]](content-model/checks.md#19-checks)` in ASC154. An agent reading the JSON can't follow them. They should be absolute or `go/` addresses, as `docs` already is.
5. **Search excerpts from a snippet source.** A match in a snippet's file prints the whole file as one line of about 600 characters (seen with `crates/ascribe-cli/tests/output/agents/quill/AGENTS.md.snap`). It should be cut around the match, as a page's excerpt is.

## Done looks like

- The summary line says what it counts, for example "checked 9 files for every build, 1 with problems: …", with `files_reported` keeping its meaning in JSON. Or the text names the scope another way, and the command reference matches.
- The rules' `@available` example uses the project's own targets, or none, and each dimension in the directive lines lists its values.
- The `new-page` wording matches what it shows, and the prompt's `path` description and `commands.md` agree with the code.
- `help` in JSON has no relative links (a test over `diagnostics.toml` holds it).
- A snippet source's search excerpt is cut to the same length as a page's.
- Re-blessed outputs reviewed; `changes/` entries where a user would notice.

From the agent-writer persona review: [Ascribe for agent writers](https://claude.ai/artifact/EvMjSQunHmV6Fvj5LQfB1o), the "smaller things" table.

content.body:
"What changed?" and "is this fixed in my version?" are common questions for an agent. But `/changelog/` (`site/src/pages/changelog.astro`) has no Markdown version, no `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`, and no entry in the docs' `llms.txt`. With `Accept: text/markdown`, the edge function finds no `/changelog.md` and answers with the 2,300-line HTML page of collapsed `<details>`. The only other source is `CHANGELOG.md` on GitHub, which leaves out the entries in `changes/` that aren't gathered yet. The site shows those.

## Done looks like

- The site publishes `/changelog.md`: the same releases and entries the page shows, the unreleased ones included, as CommonMark, with release headings anchored as on the page (`#v0.4.4`).
- The page's head links to it with `rel="alternate" type="text/markdown"`, and the edge function answers `/changelog/` asked for as Markdown with it (`site/test/negotiation.test.ts`).
- An agent reading the docs can find it. Either the docs' `llms.txt` lists it (for example under an "Optional" section, the way the llms.txt format allows), or the pointer on each page names it. Which one is the PR's call, since `llms.txt` is written from the docs project and the changelog isn't in it.
- `site/README.md` says where it comes from.

Not overlapping #970, which reshapes the entries themselves. A shorter changelog makes this file cheaper for an agent to read too.

From the agent-reader review, [Ascribe's docs, read by an agent](https://claude.ai/artifact/CTJjJSgG38ChxgJhSCUvbo), finding F3.

content.body:
An agent that reads the HTML, not the Markdown version, usually runs it through an HTML-to-text or HTML-to-Markdown converter. Two pieces of the site output are lost in that conversion:

- **Tab labels.** `<ascribe-tab value="npm" label="npm">` has its label only in an attribute. Without the script it's shown as CSS generated content (`packages/elements/src/tabs.ts`), and with it as a button the script adds. A converter gets neither, so `getting-started/` reads as two `npm`/`pnpm` code blocks with nothing saying which is which. The `.md` handles this well ("Package manager: npm" headings), but an agent that only has the HTML gets it wrong.
- **Code languages.** Astro's Shiki output marks a block's language as `data-language="sh"`. Converters (Turndown, html2text, readability-based fetchers) read `class="language-sh"` on the `<code>`, so the fences come out with no language.

## Done looks like

- Each tab's label is text in the DOM that a converter reads before the tab's content, hidden from sight while the script's buttons show it. For example, a visually hidden element, or the label as a heading-like first child that the script hides. Screen readers announce it once, not twice, which the e2e test checks.
- Code blocks the site output gives Astro carry `class="language-<lang>"` on `<code>`, through the integration's Shiki transformer, so it's the same in `astro dev` and the built site.
- `packages/elements/CONTRACT.md` §3 and the fixtures in `tests/render/` change together, since both renderers must agree. It's a contract change, so it has its decision.
- A test converts a built page with tabs to text (any common converter) and finds each label before its block.

From the agent-reader review, [Ascribe's docs, read by an agent](https://claude.ai/artifact/CTJjJSgG38ChxgJhSCUvbo), finding F7.

Calling `ascribe_resolve` with `{"project": "docs", "page": "docs/content/install.md"}` returns this error:

> `project` goes with a `page` of `go:<name>`: a page finds its project
> Paths are read from the server's working directory, /workspace/ascribe.

That's true, but an agent has to work out that the fix is to drop `project`. Most will retry with other paths first. `ascribe_search` and `ascribe_refs` take `project` with other arguments, so passing it here is a natural guess.

## Done looks like

- The error says what to send: "Leave out `project` when `page` is a path; the page's project is found from it", and, when `page` resolves to a file, the call to make (`{"page": "docs/content/install.md"}`).
- Or the tool accepts `project` with a path when the path is inside that project, and errors only when it isn't. The PR picks one.
- A test in the MCP tests covers the case.

The README's "Built for agents" bullet says agents that read the docs "get `llms.txt`, a Markdown version of every page, and JSON". A site built with `@ascribed/astro` publishes the first two, plus `/go/<name>.json` for each permalink. It doesn't publish the page JSON the build writes (`format: "ascribe-page"`, with headings, availability, and the resolved tree). content.body:
`ascribe search` prints each match's block as its excerpt, with `…` at the ends of a paragraph. A code block is matched as one block, and its excerpt isn't cut to the match. In the docs project:

```
$ ascribe search "fail on warnings in CI" --limit 5 | wc -c
20114
```

Of those 20,114 bytes, 14,701 are one line: the JSON Schema in `content/_generated/json-check.md`, flattened, because it has the words somewhere in its 400 lines. The useful hit, `getting-started.md:114` ("add --deny-warnings to fail on warnings too"), is 100 bytes. `ascribe_search` returns the same over MCP, twice: in `content` and in `structuredContent.concise`. So an agent pays about 10k tokens for one answer.

## Done looks like

- An excerpt is at most about 240 characters around the first matched word, for every kind of block, a code block or a table included, with `…` where it's cut. In JSON, the place keeps its line and range so the agent can read more.
- A code block's match reports the line within the block where the first word is, not only the block's first line.
- A test holds the docs' "fail on warnings in CI" (or a fixture with a long code block) to that bound.
- Whether generated fragments (`_generated/`) are searched at all is decided in the PR. They're included in pages, so readers do see them.

Separate from #992, which finds near matches when no block has every word.

From the agent-reader review, [Ascribe's docs, read by an agent](https://claude.ai/artifact/CTJjJSgG38ChxgJhSCUvbo), finding F6.

content.body:
Follow-up to #948 (PR #1049).

After #1049 removes quill's `self-managed-3.3` build, `ascribe versions retire "self-managed 3.4" --dry-run --url https://archive.quill.dev/3.4/` on `examples/quill` lists only one build outside the line:

```
Builds that aren't lines of self-managed change what they show:
  cloud's plain output changes install-agent.md
  cloud's site output changes install-agent.md
Rewriting them needs --force.
```

The `cloud` build filters for `cloud`, but its availability lines still show self-managed's versions: `Available: Quill Cloud (GA); self-managed (preview, 3.4+)` (and `3.3+` for the page). The retirement rewrites `self-managed preview 3.4` to `self-managed preview`, so cloud's line becomes `self-managed (preview)`. That's a visible change, so retire refuses without `--force`.

## Done looks like

Pick one, recorded as a decision:

- A build filtered for one target leaves other targets' versions out of its availability lines. Then a retirement of another target changes nothing it shows. This is an output change for every filtered build.
- Or retire's comparison ignores changes that only touch another target's part of an availability line, and says so in its output.
- Or quill's cloud build changes so it shows no self-managed versions.

After that, `versions retire "self-managed 3.4"` on quill runs without `--force`, and `crates/ascribe-cli/tests/output/versions-retire.txt` shows it.

content.body:
**The problem you're trying to solve:**

SPEC §3.3.1 (added in #1072 for #969) defines a grammar for the `key=value` pairs in a fenced code block's info string. Any word that isn't a pair is "left to the consumer, and processors don't report it." Because of that, a near-miss gets no warning:

- `phrases = true` or `title = "x"`, with spaces around `=`
- an unclosed quote, such as `title="connect.ts`
- a hand-written title with a quote escaped once. `title="say \"hi\""` worked before #1072. Now CommonMark removes the backslash, the word becomes `title="say "hi""`, it isn't a pair, and the title disappears. To keep the quote, the page has to write `\\\"` (or `\\"`).
- a known key that isn't lowercase, such as `Title=x`
- a pair written as the first word (```` ```title="x.ts" ````). §3.3.1 reads that as a block with no language and a title, but comrak's `data-meta` and Astro's `meta` both start after the first word, so the site shows no caption. `code-language-missing` already flags this block, but its message doesn't mention the pair.

In every one of these cases, the author meant a pair, and the block quietly loses its title, its phrases, or its example marker.

**What you'd like Ascribe to do:**

Add a check, warning by default, for a word after the language that starts like one of the pairs a processor reads (`phrases`, `title`, `tested`, `request`, `response`, matched case-insensitively and followed by optional spaces and `=`) but doesn't parse as a pair under `ascribe_core::info_string`. Where the fix is clear, the message says what to write, for example "write a quote in a title as `\\\"`". If possible, it offers that fix. Words that don't start with one of these keys, such as `{1,3}` or `showLineNumbers`, stay unreported.

**Done when:**

- §3.3.1 says that a processor reports a word that starts with a known key but isn't a pair, instead of saying that processors don't report it. This changes SPEC.md, so it needs Kyle's OK on the wording.
- A new diagnostic covers each near-miss listed above, using `ascribe_core::info_string` to decide what counts as a pair.
- `code-language-missing`'s message mentions it when the first word is a pair.
- Conformance cases cover each near-miss and a clean block, and the change comes with a changelog entry.

Follow-up from the review of #1072.

content.body:
From #953's product decision: each diagnostic entry's header line, such as "Error · file level · next step: choose", keeps its compact form, and each word in it links to its definition in the diagnostics reference. #1081 (the glossary PR) added the sections those links point at: [Severity](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/docs/content/checks/diagnostics.md#severity), **File level and page level**, and **What to do next**. It left the links out because they don't fit the docs' own `page-size` limit for agents (50,000 characters of Markdown).

Each link costs about 55 characters in the agent Markdown. Built with links on every entry (generator: `write_entry` in `tests/conformance/tests/docs.rs`):

| Page | Now | With links |
|---|---|---|
| Links, pages, and sources (`checks/diagnostics/pages.md`, 67 entries) | ~47,400 | ~61,600 |
| The content model (`content-model.md`, 59) | under 50,000 | ~50,900 |
| Content checks (`content-checks.md`, 39) | ~42,500 | ~52,600 |

Kyle chose to split these pages first, then add the links (decision in the #953 project thread, 26 October 2026).

## Done looks like

- The three pages are split so that each page stays under 50,000 characters with the links in, and `ascribe check --deny-warnings --config docs` reports no `page-size` advice. The diagnostics reference's list of pages names the new ones. Entries keep their `ASC` permalinks, and any page that moves or goes is recorded in `ascribe.addresses`.
- Each entry's header line links its severity to `#severity`, its level to `#file-level-and-page-level`, its next step to `#what-to-do-next`, "configurable" to `#setting-a-checks-level`, and "acknowledged" to the glossary's `acknowledgement` term, regenerated with `ASCRIBE_BLESS=1 cargo test -p ascribe-conformance --test docs`.
